title: Lecture 4 — Numerical Computing with NumPy
text:
14.1 Step Size Selection
Choosing the right time step dt is crucial:
Too large: - Inaccurate results - May violate constraints (e.g., negative populations) - Numerical instability
Too small: - Slow computation - Accumulated rounding errors
Rule of thumb: For Euler’s method, dt should be much smaller than the characteristic time scale of the system.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Demonstrate instability
def sir_with_checks(S0, I0, R0, beta, gamma, t_max, dt):
    """SIR with checks for negative values"""
    N = S0 + I0 + R0
    n_steps = int(t_max / dt)
    
    t = np.arange(n_steps) * dt
    S = np.zeros(n_steps)
    I = np.zeros(n_steps)
    R = np.zeros(n_steps)
    
    S[0], I[0], R[0] = S0, I0, R0
    
    for step in range(1, n_steps):
        state = np.array([S[step-1], I[step-1], R[step-1]])
        derivs = sir_derivatives(t[step-1], state, beta, gamma, N)
        
        S[step] = S[step-1] + derivs[0] * dt
        I[step] = I[step-1] + derivs[1] * dt
        R[step] = R[step-1] + derivs[2] * dt
        
        # Check for violations
        if S[step] < 0 or I[step] < 0 or R[step] < 0:
            print(f"Warning: Negative population at step {step} (t={t[step]:.1f})")
            print(f"S={S[step]:.2f}, I={I[step]:.2f}, R={R[step]:.2f}")
            break
    
    return t, S, I, R

# Test with large dt
print("Testing with dt=5:")
t, S, I, R = sir_with_checks(990, 10, 0, 0.5, 0.1, 100, 5)

print("\nTesting with dt=1:")
t, S, I, R = sir_with_checks(990, 10, 0, 0.5, 0.1, 100, 1)

14.2 Conservation Laws
For the SIR model, \(N = S + I + R\) should be constant. Check this!

import numpy as np

def sir_with_conservation_check(S0, I0, R0, beta, gamma, t_max, dt):
    """SIR with conservation checking"""
    N = S0 + I0 + R0
    t, S, I, R = simulate_sir(S0, I0, R0, beta, gamma, t_max, dt)
    
    # Check conservation
    total = S + I + R
    conservation_error = np.abs(total - N)
    
    max_error = np.max(conservation_error)
    mean_error = np.mean(conservation_error)
    
    print(f"Conservation check:")
    print(f"Max error: {max_error:.6e}")
    print(f"Mean error: {mean_error:.6e}")
    print(f"Relative error: {max_error/N:.6e}")
    
    return t, S, I, R

t, S, I, R = sir_with_conservation_check(990, 10, 0, 0.5, 0.1, 160, 1)

text:
14.3 Using Professional Solvers
For production code, use scipy’s ODE solvers:

import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def sir_system(t, state, beta, gamma, N):
    """SIR system for scipy"""
    S, I, R = state
    infection_rate = beta * S * I / N
    recovery_rate = gamma * I
    
    dS = -infection_rate
    dI = infection_rate - recovery_rate
    dR = recovery_rate
    
    return [dS, dI, dR]

# Initial conditions
N = 1000
state0 = [990, 10, 0]  # [S0, I0, R0]
beta, gamma = 0.5, 0.1
t_span = (0, 160)

# Solve using adaptive solver
solution = solve_ivp(
    sir_system,
    t_span,
    state0,
    args=(beta, gamma, N),
    dense_output=True,
    method='RK45'  # 4th/5th order Runge-Kutta
)

# Evaluate at specific times
t = np.linspace(0, 160, 161)
S, I, R = solution.sol(t)

# Plot
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(t, S, label='Susceptible', linewidth=2)
plt.plot(t, I, label='Infectious', linewidth=2)
plt.plot(t, R, label='Recovered', linewidth=2)
plt.xlabel('Time (days)')
plt.ylabel('Population')
plt.title('SIR Model (using scipy.integrate.solve_ivp)')
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.show()

print(f"Solution successful: {solution.success}")
print(f"Number of evaluations: {solution.nfev}")

16.3 Copy vs. View Issues

import numpy as np

# Surprising behavior
arr = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
slice1 = arr[1:4]
slice2 = arr[1:4]

slice1[0] = 999

print(f"slice2: {slice2}")  # Also changed!

slice_copy[0] = 999

16.4 Boolean Array Pitfalls

import numpy as np

text:
Course Description
This course provides a fast-paced introduction to programming and computational methods for graduate study in mathematics and statistics. We will use Python and R to develop practical programming skills while also introducing fundamental ideas from computer science, numerical computing, data management, and reproducible research.
The course emphasizes problem solving and computational thinking rather than memorization of language syntax. Topics include programming fundamentals, data structures, algorithms, numerical representation and error, data manipulation and visualization, simulation, statistical computing, software organization, version control, testing and debugging, and reproducible computational workflows.
An important goal is to prepare students not only to write programs for this course, but also to approach computational problems effectively in subsequent coursework, research, and professional settings. We will therefore discuss practices used in real computational work, including organizing projects, managing dependencies and data, writing maintainable code, testing programs, documenting work, and using Git and GitHub.
The course uses Python and R throughout. Students will generally learn concepts first through Python and then see how similar computational ideas are expressed in R.

title: MATH 5200: Computing Using R & Python
text:
Course Project
The semester project is a substantial computational investigation of a topic chosen by the student in consultation with the instructor.
Projects may involve:

data analysis;
simulation;
numerical computation;
algorithmic experiments;
statistical modeling; or
another computational project approved by the instructor.

The project will develop through several stages:

Proposal
Preliminary analysis / computational development
Final analysis and final product
Presentation

The purpose of the project is to give students an opportunity to work on a problem of genuine interest while practicing the complete computational workflow developed in the course.
A separate project description provides detailed requirements, examples, and guidance for selecting a topic.

Academic Integrity
Everything submitted for a grade must represent the student’s own work, except for clearly acknowledged and appropriately cited material from other sources or assistance explicitly permitted by the instructor.
Students may discuss homework and projects with classmates unless an assignment specifies otherwise, but they should not copy another student’s work.
Examinations and other assessments designated as individual work may have substantially more restrictive collaboration and resource rules. Those rules will be stated explicitly when the assessment is assigned.
Students are responsible for understanding and following Georgetown University’s academic integrity policies.
